extracted.intended_audience: NPR listeners and general readers interested in media and journalism ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations for evaluating the role, behavior, and management of network news anchors in light of credibility scandals (using the Brian Williams case as exemplar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The story's collapse corrodes trust in the anchor, in NBC and in the greater profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Williams' false claim that a rocket-propelled grenade struck his helicopter in Iraq is cited as eroding trust. Past scandals (plagiarized stories, made-up stories, unreliable sources) are noted as comparable harms. Assess how an anchor's individual falsehoods affect audience confidence in both the person and the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchors should not be the story
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an overall trend, in television news particularly, toward making the reporters and the anchors the story rather than having them report the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid marketing anchors as stars in ways that shift focus from reported events to personalities. Production and publicity choices should keep attention on the story, not the anchor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and fact verification
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations must guard against stories that were plagiarized, made up, or based on unreliable sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial processes should verify personal anecdotes and reporting claims as rigorously as other reporting. The Williams example shows how unverified personal recollections can become a major credibility problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and decisiveness of executive response
rubrics_metrics.description: How quickly and firmly executives act when misconduct or falsehoods surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece criticizes NBC for taking nearly a week to suspend Williams and allowing him to set his own terms. Rapid, transparent action is implied as the correct managerial response to protect organizational credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation from conflicts of interest and undue influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives' personal relationships with anchors should not affect disciplinary or ethical decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joe Scarborough's on-air speculation about Williams' relationship with Comcast/NBC executives (Steve Burke) is cited as raising questions about favoritism. Policies should guard against perceived or real preferential treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of an anchor's indispensability to newscasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Questioning how essential a marquee anchor is to the success of a newscast and whether a less-known anchor could fill the role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although high salaries reflect executives' belief in anchors' centrality ('law of supply and demand'), networks should consider experiments and succession planning rather than assuming a single personality is irreplaceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding mindless adulation / star worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Networks and audiences are complicit in the excessive adulation attached to anchors, which can distort coverage and judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to how promotion and audience culture elevate anchors; reduce hero-worship that can insulate talent from accountability and shift reporting priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and appropriate consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Misconduct by anchors should be met with clear accountability (suspension, removal, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Williams' suspension and speculation about six months without pay; the Dan Rather case as precedent for forcing out an anchor after botched reporting. Consequences should be proportionate, transparent, and consistently applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial oversight to keep the camera focused on the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and producers must ensure that fame or persona does not lead to self-centered presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As Westin asks: 'Are we making sure that no matter how famous our anchors and our reporters are, they're keeping the camera focused on the story rather than on themselves?' Implement production standards and editorial checks to enforce this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of material impact on public understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether a false claim materially affects the public's understanding of a story, while recognizing that even immaterial falsehoods can erode trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Williams' tall tale was 'not itself particularly important to the public's understanding of the overall story of the war in Iraq,' yet still corrosive. Distinguish between factual significance and reputational harm when deciding responses.
